feature: Soft gradients in a recording play smooth
summary: A recording of a dark soft gradient (a translucent terminal window, a sheet's material) now plays, scrubs and shows in the editor as a smooth ramp instead of visible bands. Words, window edges and lines are left exactly as they were. Recording itself is untouched.
setup: Photonz Dev, release Next, no flag changed from its default. Walk: Scripts/playtest/soft-gradients-in-a-recording-play-smooth-walk.json (banded fixture). Your own file was run through the same walk with its path swapped in.

try.do: Open Recording 2026-11-16 at 06.33.31 (the one you sent) from History or with File > Open. The picture here is the banded test recording at Next defaults; yours is shown cropped in the next two steps.
Look at the empty sidebar of the terminal window in the frame: the dark gradient has no hard band edges.
Compare the three strips, contrast stretched 14x and enlarged: QuickTime playing the file, Photonz with the switch off, Photonz at Next defaults.
Press Space to play and scrub the playhead: the gradient stays smooth while it moves.
Watch the before and after clip: red square is off, green square is on.
Read some terminal text up close in the frame: it is as sharp as before.

evaluate: On your display, does the terminal's sidebar read as one smooth gradient now when you play the recording in Photonz?
Can you see the fine grain in the smoothed areas at normal viewing distance? It is up to one shade either way and only where a band was.
Does anything that should be sharp (text, a hairline, a window edge) look softer to you?
Is it fine that exporting at the top quality still copies the file as recorded, with its steps, until exports can be written in 10-bit?
rough: Reproduced on your files before anything changed: the frame at 3 s, x 261, y 740 to 2040, has 27 ten-bit levels with flat runs up to 124 px (11 eight-bit levels, 161 px); the screenshot before it has 11 levels and 164 px. The screen itself is drawn in 8-bit steps.
On screen in Photonz (window capture, 8 px means down that strip): 40 levels, longest flat run 8 to 26 px, against 103 to 137 px with the switch off. The bar was under 40 px and 35 levels: met.

Unit tests on a controlled 10-shade staircase over 1300 px: deep output under 40 px flat and 35+ levels; 8-bit output's row means pass the same bar; a flat area and every edge pixel come back bit for bit; a one-shade hairline survives.

Sharp things: terminal text in the same frames, on against off, 0.002% of edge pixels differ, 99th percentile 0 ten-bit codes; mean colours of the sidebar and the text block within 1 ten-bit code (Delta E well under 1).

Cost: GPU kernel time about +1.0 ms for a full 3456x2234 frame (1.4 against 0.4 ms) and +0.2 ms at half size, median over 37 real frames; readings on this shared Mac swung 2x between runs. Playing the 6 minute reference edit for a minute: 1 frame missed of 1818 both on and off; scrub lag 2 frames median, 4 worst, both ways; time to the first sharp frame of a 3456 recording 1007 to 1072 ms on, 1035 to 1073 ms off.

Recording is untouched: the capture code is not in the diff. Start drill, 6 runs: median 8.7 ms from Return to first frame (9.6 ms measured this morning before the change). No existing drill counts dropped capture frames over a minute, so that number is not measured here; the 60 s stop drill passes every budget.

Not done, and why this task stays open: exports. Your file plays smooth only inside Photonz. A High export of an untouched or cut-only recording copies the file (0.1 s), so QuickTime and Safari still show the steps. At Standard the grain does not survive H.264's budget: the file read as banded (94 px against 95 px flat) in twice the time (11.2 s against 5.4 s), so Standard and Small exports are not smoothed (5.4 s, as before). High drawn exports (an edit with titles) are smoothed; an encoder test at High's 55 Mbps kept a 31 px flat run. A smooth file for other players needs a 10-bit export; left in this task's log for the next pass.

A small recording shown larger than itself (the 1280 wide fixture at 1.5x) smooths less on screen: longest flat run 39 to 41 px against 155 px off, because enlarging blends some of the grain. Your recordings are shown smaller than they were recorded, where it holds well.
